mcqs.question: What's the correct way to match an eviction policy to an access pattern?
options: Always use LRU since it has the simplest implementation
LRU for recency-driven access, LFU for a stable hot set where popularity is sustained over time, TTL for time-bound relevance
Always use LFU since it more accurately reflects true popularity
Eviction policy doesn't matter as long as the cache is large enough
mcqs.explanation: Each policy encodes a different assumption about what predicts future access — recency, accumulated frequency, or a hard time limit — and the right one depends on which assumption actually matches the workload. Simplicity alone doesn't justify LRU when the pattern doesn't fit it, LFU isn't universally better (it costs more bookkeeping and adapts more slowly), and cache size doesn't make the eviction policy's mismatch with the access pattern go away.

mcqs.question: Under pure LRU, why can a key that's read 1,000 times a day get evicted in favor of a one-time viral read?
options: LRU always keeps the most frequently accessed keys regardless of recency
This scenario can only happen if the cache size is set to zero
LRU tracks only recency of access, not frequency, so a one-time read that happened more recently looks identical to sustained popularity from LRU's perspective
LFU would make the exact same eviction decision as LRU in this exact scenario
mcqs.explanation: LRU's signal is purely "when was this last touched," which can't distinguish a single recent viral read from years of steady daily access — both simply look "recently used." LRU explicitly ignores frequency, this failure happens at any realistic cache size once it's full, and LFU would correctly favor the high-frequency key instead, which is exactly why it's the fix for this scenario.

mcqs.question: What's the real cost of choosing LFU over LRU?
options: LFU has no downside compared to LRU and should always be preferred
LRU requires more bookkeeping per access than LFU does
LFU adapts to genuinely shifting access patterns faster than LRU does
LFU tracks true popularity better, but costs more bookkeeping per access, and without a decay mechanism can be slower to adapt when access patterns genuinely shift
mcqs.explanation: LFU's per-key counters cost more to maintain than LRU's simple recency ordering, and without decaying old counts, a key that was popular last month can keep blocking eviction long after it's gone cold — a real adaptability cost. LRU is the cheaper one to maintain, not LFU, and LRU reacts to changing patterns faster precisely because it has no memory of past popularity to overcome.

mcqs.question: A team picks LRU "because it's the standard eviction policy" without checking the workload. What's the risk?
options: It skips checking whether the access pattern actually fits LRU's assumption that recency predicts future access — for a trending or viral-prone workload, that assumption breaks down and hurts the hit rate
LRU is never an appropriate choice for any production cache
This problem only occurs when the cache uses a hash-based eviction implementation
LRU and LFU produce identical eviction decisions in every scenario, so the choice never actually matters
mcqs.explanation: "Standard" describes how common a policy is, not whether it fits this workload's actual access pattern — and for a trending or viral-prone cache, LRU's core assumption breaks down in a measurable, harmful way. LRU is genuinely the right choice for plenty of workloads, the mismatch has nothing to do with the eviction data structure's implementation, and the two policies clearly diverge in cases like the viral-read scenario.
